title: F-1 Fixed-Admission Rule Takes Effect September 15: What Indian Students Must Do
excerpt: A DHS final rule replaces decades-old duration-of-status admissions with a fixed 'admit until date' on the Form I-94 - after which students must extend their stay or depart.
body:
• Starting September 15, 2026, most F-1 students entering the United States will receive a fixed Admit Until Date on their Form I-94 instead of "duration of status."
  • Admission will run to the program end date on the student's I-20 — capped at four years — plus a 30-day departure period, down from the old 60-day grace period.
  • Students who need more time to finish their program, start a new one, or take up OPT must apply for an Extension of Stay with USCIS, or depart and seek readmission.
  • Current students admitted under the old system get transition protections: they may remain until their I-20 program end date or valid OPT ends, not beyond November 14, 2030.

A Fundamental Change to Student Admissions

After more than three decades, the way international students are admitted to the United States changes this month. Under a Department of Homeland Security final rule published July 17, 2026, most individuals entering in F-1 status on or after September 15, 2026 will be admitted until a specific date — the Admit Until Date, or AUD, on their Form I-94 — rather than for "duration of status," according to guidance from Yale University's Office of International Students & Scholars. The AUD is generally the program end date on the student's I-20, capped at four years, plus 30 days to depart.

Once the period of admission expires, students who need additional time generally must obtain another lawful period of authorized stay before the current one ends — either through international travel and readmission, or by filing for an Extension of Stay with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Context & Background

Duration of Status has been the admissions framework for F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors since the early 1990s. Instead of a fixed expiration date, their I-94s simply read "D/S," and lawful stay was tied to maintaining status: making normal progress toward the academic program, keeping a valid SEVIS record, and following enrollment and employment rules.

The old system was flexible: if a student needed extra time — for dissertation research or moving from a bachelor's to a master's — the school's Designated School Official could extend the I-20 without any USCIS application. Beginning September 15, that campus-level flexibility is replaced by a federal deadline on every student's record. J-1 exchange visitors and F-2 and J-2 dependents get fixed admission periods too.

Impact & Analysis

The most immediate practical change: the Form I-94 becomes one of a student's most important immigration documents. Check it after every entry to confirm the Admit Until Date is accurate — remaining past it without action means accruing unlawful presence.

"F students who need additional time to complete their program of study, begin a new program of study, or to engage in post-completion optional practical training (OPT) or science, technology, engineering and mathematics OPT must apply for an extension of stay with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or depart the United States and obtain a new period of admission from U.S. Customs and Border Protection upon reentry."

— U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States FAQ

The rule also tightens the edges of student life. The post-program grace period shrinks from 60 days to 30. New restrictions apply to transfers, changes of educational objective, and lateral or reverse matriculation. English-language training is capped at 24 months of admission; public high schools at an aggregate of 12 months.

One misconception is worth clearing up: four years is not a lifetime limit. The rule caps a single period of admission — doctoral students and long-term scholars can stay longer, but must secure an additional authorized stay through an Extension of Stay or travel and reentry before the current one expires.

Diaspora Angle

The Indian diaspora feels this rule directly: students and families plan multi-year degrees and significant financial commitments around a stable immigration framework, and that framework just got a hard expiration date. For those already in the United States, Yale's guidance is reassuring: "for many current students and scholars, nothing changes immediately on September 15, 2026." But anyone traveling internationally after the rule takes effect will be readmitted under the new system — so check the new AUD and talk to the school's international office before booking.

What's Next

Implementation guidance is still being written. DHS, USCIS, Customs and Border Protection, and the Student and Exchange Visitor Program are expected to issue clarifications in the coming weeks, and universities are preparing Extension of Stay resources to have ready before September 15. Watch the Congressional Review Act window too: any move by Congress to delay or overturn the rule would be announced in the Federal Register.

The practical checklist: know your program end date, check your I-94 after every entry, and build Extension of Stay timelines into any program change or OPT plans.
nri_angle: Indian students and their families plan multi-year degrees around a stable immigration framework that now carries a hard expiration date - and any international travel after September 15 means readmission under the new fixed-date system.
